stages.title: Molecular biology
stages.hook: Your cells hold a molecule over 2 metres long if stretched out, yet it fits in a nucleus a few micrometres wide. How is information stored in it, and how is it used?
explain: DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel strands. Each strand is a chain of nucleotides: a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate and one of four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). The strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases: A pairs with T and G pairs with C. Hence in double-stranded DNA, %A = %T and %G = %C.

The central dogma describes the flow of information: DNA is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein. RNA differs from DNA: it has ribose, it is usually single-stranded, and it uses uracil (U) in place of thymine. Proteins are chains of amino acids folded into shapes that determine their function.
In eukaryotes DNA is wound around histone proteins and packaged into chromosomes, which makes it compact. Humans have 46 chromosomes in most body cells (23 pairs).

example.q: A double-stranded DNA sample is 28% adenine. What percentage is guanine?
steps: A pairs with T, so T is also 28%.
A + T = 56%, leaving 44% for G + C.
G pairs with C, so G = C = 22%.

analogies.tech: DNA is like a hard drive using a four-letter code; RNA is a working copy printed out for the factory floor.
analogies.home: A recipe book stays on the shelf; you copy a recipe to the kitchen and make the dish.
analogies.music: DNA is the full score, mRNA is the part sheet and the protein is the played music.

stages.mnemonic: A-T and G-C: Apples in Trees, Cars in Garages.
terms: Building block of nucleic acids: sugar, phosphate and base.
A with T (U in RNA), G with C.
Making an RNA copy of a gene.

misc.right: DNA is transcribed into RNA, which ribosomes translate into protein. Proteins are made by ribosomes, not by DNA.

stages.limits: The central dogma has exceptions, such as retroviruses that copy RNA into DNA, and many RNAs that are never translated.

teach.model: DNA holds the instructions as a sequence of four bases. A gene is copied into mRNA by transcription. Ribosomes then read the mRNA in groups of three bases, each coding an amino acid, and join them into a protein by translation.

stages.title: DNA replication and gene expression
stages.hook: Before a cell divides it must copy 3 billion base pairs with about one error per billion bases. How can such accurate copying happen?
explain: DNA replication is semi-conservative: each new DNA molecule has one old strand and one new strand. Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks hydrogen bonds. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to each template by complementary base pairing, building new strands only in the 5' to 3' direction. Ligase seals gaps. Polymerases proofread and repair errors, which keeps the error rate very low.

Gene expression has two steps. In transcription, RNA polymerase reads the template strand of a gene and builds mRNA. In eukaryotes, introns are spliced out and exons joined. In translation, ribosomes read mRNA codons (three bases each). tRNA molecules with matching anticodons bring amino acids. AUG is the start codon and also codes for methionine. UAA, UAG and UGA are stop codons.

Not all genes are active in every cell. Gene regulation turns genes on and off, for instance by transcription factors binding near a gene, so a muscle cell and a nerve cell use the same DNA but make different proteins. Mutations change the DNA sequence: substitutions may be silent, missense or nonsense, while insertions or deletions that are not multiples of three cause frameshifts.

example.q: An mRNA reads AUG GCU UUU UAA. Which amino acids are added, given that GCU is alanine (Ala), UUU is phenylalanine (Phe) and AUG is methionine (Met)?
steps: UAA is a stop codon, so no amino acid is added.

analogies.tech: Replication is photocopying a whole book; transcription is photocopying one chapter to take to the workshop.
analogies.home: Reading a recipe three ingredients at a time is like reading codons.
analogies.music: Splicing is like editing out the pauses of a recording and joining the good parts.

misc.right: Many mutations are silent or neutral. Some are harmful and a few are beneficial.

stages.title: Enzymes and metabolism
stages.hook: Starch in your mouth turns to sugar within minutes, but in a test tube without saliva it takes years. What does saliva contain that changes the speed?
explain: Enzymes are protein catalysts that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. Each enzyme has an active site whose shape fits its substrate, so enzymes are specific. The induced-fit model says the active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds.

Rate depends on conditions. Raising temperature increases collisions until the optimum; beyond it the enzyme denatures (its shape changes irreversibly). Each enzyme has an optimum pH; pepsin works in acid, amylase near neutral. More substrate raises the rate until all active sites are busy, giving a plateau at Vmax. Inhibitors reduce activity: competitive inhibitors bind to the active site, non-competitive ones bind elsewhere and change its shape.

Metabolism is all of the chemical reactions in a cell. Catabolic reactions break molecules down and release energy; anabolic reactions build molecules and use energy. Pathways are controlled by feedback inhibition, where an end product inhibits an early enzyme.

example.q: An enzyme has Vmax = 100 µmol/min and Km = 5 mM (v = Vmax × [S] ÷ (Km + [S])). What is v at [S] = 15 mM?

analogies.tech: A key (substrate) fits a lock (active site), and a lock can be jammed by the wrong key (inhibitor).
analogies.farm: A mill has a limited number of grinders: adding more grain no longer increases flour per hour.
analogies.city: A thermostat in a factory: feedback inhibition shuts off a production line when the shelves are full.

stages.mnemonic: Enzyme = Edit speed, not result: it lowers the hill, not the end point.

stages.limits: The lock-and-key model is a simplification, which is why induced fit is preferred.

stages.title: Immunology
stages.hook: A vaccine can contain a harmless piece of a germ yet protect for years. How does the body learn from a pretend attack?
explain: The body has layers of defence. Physical and chemical barriers (skin, mucus, stomach acid) are non-specific. Phagocytes engulf pathogens. The adaptive immune system is specific: each pathogen carries antigens, and lymphocytes recognise them. B cells make antibodies that bind a specific antigen; helper T cells coordinate the response; killer T cells destroy infected cells.

After first exposure, memory cells remain. On a second exposure the response is faster and stronger (secondary response). Vaccines expose the body to a harmless form of an antigen so memory cells form without illness. Herd immunity occurs when enough people are immune that spread is limited. The threshold is about 1 − 1/R₀, where R₀ is the average number of people one case infects in a fully susceptible population.
Antibiotics treat bacterial infections only. Autoimmune diseases occur when the immune system attacks the body's own cells. Allergies are over-reactions to harmless antigens.

example.q: For a disease with R₀ = 4, what fraction of the population needs to be immune for herd immunity?

analogies.city: Phagocytes are police on patrol, antibodies are guided missiles with one target, memory cells are wanted-posters kept on file.
analogies.sport: Watching a replay of the opposing team's moves prepares a team for the next match, as a vaccine does.
analogies.tech: Antivirus software keeps signatures of past threats and reacts faster to known ones.

stages.limits: Real herd-immunity thresholds depend on vaccine effectiveness, mixing patterns and variants, so 1 − 1/R₀ is an estimate.

stages.title: Human physiology
stages.hook: After a sugary snack your blood glucose barely changes much, but it can change a lot in untreated diabetes. What is controlling it?
explain: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within narrow limits using negative feedback: a receptor detects a change, a control centre processes it and an effector acts to reverse the change. Blood glucose is controlled by the pancreas: insulin lowers it by promoting uptake and storage as glycogen, and glucagon raises it by releasing glucose from glycogen. In type 1 diabetes the pancreas makes too little insulin; in type 2, cells respond poorly to insulin.

The nervous system sends rapid electrical impulses along neurons. A reflex arc is receptor → sensory neuron → relay neuron → motor neuron → effector. Hormones act more slowly through the blood and last longer. The heart's output is cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.

The kidneys filter blood in nephrons, reabsorb useful substances and excrete urea in urine. ADH from the pituitary gland increases water reabsorption when the body is dehydrated, so urine becomes more concentrated.

example.q: A person's heart rate is 70 beats per minute and stroke volume is 70 mL. What is cardiac output?
steps: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.

stages.title: Microbiology
stages.hook: A single bacterium on a petri dish becomes a visible colony overnight. How fast do bacteria grow, and what limits them?
explain: Bacteria are prokaryotes with a cell wall made of peptidoglycan, DNA in a nucleoid region, and often plasmids (small rings of DNA). They reproduce by binary fission. In ideal conditions the number doubles every generation time, so growth is exponential: N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of generations.

A growth curve in a closed culture has four phases: lag (adjusting), log (exponential), stationary (growth equals death, as nutrients run out and wastes build up) and death. Gram staining separates bacteria into Gram-positive (thick wall, purple) and Gram-negative (thin wall with outer membrane, pink), which helps in choosing treatment.

Bacteria exchange genes by conjugation, transformation and transduction. Plasmids can carry antibiotic resistance genes, so resistance can spread between bacteria. Viruses are not cells: they have a protein coat around genetic material and need a host to replicate. Aseptic technique prevents contamination in cultures.

example.q: A culture has 1000 bacteria with a generation time of 20 minutes. How many bacteria after 2 hours (ideal conditions)?

analogies.tech: Exponential growth is like a chain message forwarded to two friends each time.
analogies.farm: Fermenting yogurt: warm milk lets bacteria grow quickly, then acid builds up and slows them.
analogies.city: A city grows fast until space and food run out: the stationary phase.

stages.mnemonic: Lag, Log, Stationary, Death: Large Lizards Sleep Deeply.

questions.q: A hospital finds an infection resistant to several antibiotics. Which mechanism could spread resistance quickly?
o: A plasmid carrying resistance genes passed between bacteria
Mitosis in the human cells of the patient
Sunlight shining through the ward windows
Antibodies passed between the bacteria
questions.why: Plasmids move horizontally between cells.

questions.q: Why does a bacterial culture in a closed flask stop growing, even though it started exponentially?
questions.model: Nutrients become depleted and waste products accumulate, so growth slows until births equal deaths (stationary phase) and then deaths exceed births.
questions.why: Limited resources constrain growth.

questions.q: Why is aseptic technique important in a microbiology lab?
o: To avoid contaminating cultures and to protect the worker
To make bacteria grow faster in the dish
To kill all the useful bacteria in the room
To change the DNA of the cultures on purpose
questions.why: It prevents unwanted microorganisms from entering or leaving.

panel.q: Why are antibiotics that target peptidoglycan synthesis relatively safe for humans?
o: Human cells do not have peptidoglycan walls
Humans are immune to every kind of antibiotic
Humans are really a type of bacteria
They also kill human cells just as well as bacteria
panel.why: The target is specific to bacteria.

panel.q: A virus has no ribosomes. What does this mean for its protein production?
o: It must use a host's ribosomes
It cannot be made at all outside a cell
It makes its own ribosomes inside the capsid
It needs no proteins to reproduce
panel.why: Viruses hijack host machinery.

panel.q: A food manufacturer wants to slow bacterial growth. Which method is expected to help?
o: Refrigeration
Warm storage
Adding nutrients
Adding water and warmth
panel.why: Low temperatures slow enzymes and growth.

teach.model: Each bacterium divides into two by binary fission, so the population doubles every generation time. That is exponential growth. In a closed culture it slows and stops when nutrients run out and wastes build up.

points.ask: How do bacteria multiply?
What does the growth look like?
Why can't it go on forever?

stages.title: Ecology and population dynamics
stages.hook: Rabbits introduced to a new continent had no predators and spread rapidly. What decides how big a population can get?
explain: A population is a group of the same species in one area. Its size changes by births and immigration (adding) and deaths and emigration (removing). Under ideal conditions growth is exponential, but resources are limited, so growth slows near the carrying capacity (K), the maximum population the environment can support, giving an S-shaped (logistic) curve.

Limiting factors can be density-dependent (competition, predation, disease) or density-independent (fire, floods, severe weather). Predator and prey numbers often rise and fall in linked cycles. Ecologists estimate populations by quadrats for plants and slow animals, and by mark–release–recapture for mobile animals: N = (M × C) ÷ R, where M is the number marked first, C the second catch and R the number of marked animals recaptured.

Energy flows through ecosystems: usually only about 10% passes to the next trophic level, the rest is lost in respiration, waste and heat. This limits the length of food chains. Nutrients such as carbon and nitrogen cycle between organisms and the environment.

example.q: 40 fish are marked and released. Later 50 are caught, of which 10 are marked. Estimate the population.

analogies.farm: A field can feed only so many cows before the grass is overgrazed: carrying capacity.
analogies.city: A city's growth slows when housing and jobs run short.
analogies.sea: Overfishing removes more fish than births can replace.

terms: Maximum population size an environment can sustain.
A resource or condition that restricts population growth.
A feeding position in a food chain.
A square frame used to sample organisms in an area.

misc.wrong: A population can keep increasing exponentially for a long time.
misc.right: Resource limits eventually slow growth, usually leading to a plateau near the carrying capacity.

trip.prompt: Find an S-shaped growth curve and mark where growth is fastest.

questions.q: What does carrying capacity mean?
o: The maximum population an environment can support
The number of births per year in a population
The total weight of all the animals in a population
The total number of species in the whole world
questions.why: It is set by resources and other limits.

questions.q: 30 animals are marked. A second sample of 60 contains 6 marked animals. Estimate the population size.
Producers contain 20 000 kJ of energy. Assuming 10% transfer at each level, how much reaches secondary consumers (two transfers)?
Which method is most suitable for estimating the number of a slow-moving or fixed species such as daisies in a field?
o: Random quadrat sampling
Mark–release–recapture
Radio tracking
Counting every one by satellite
questions.why: Quadrats sample fixed or slow organisms; mark–recapture suits mobile animals.

questions.q: A population of 500 grows by 10% each year. What is its size after 2 years?
Which is a density-dependent factor?
o: Disease spreading among crowded animals
A volcanic eruption destroying a habitat
A flood sweeping through a valley
A frost killing the plants in winter
questions.why: Disease spreads faster at higher density.

questions.q: Which organisms are the primary consumers in a grassland?
o: Grass-eating animals such as zebra
Grass and other green plants
Lions and other big hunters
Fungi that break down dead matter
questions.why: Primary consumers eat producers.

questions.q: Order the phases of an S-shaped growth curve.
questions.why: Growth accelerates, then slows as limits act.

questions.q: A mark–recapture study releases marked animals that then die at a higher rate because the mark makes them visible to predators. How would this affect the estimate?
o: It would overestimate the population
It would underestimate the population
No effect
It would equal zero
questions.why: Fewer marked animals are recaptured (R smaller), so N = (M × C) ÷ R is too large.

questions.q: Why are food chains rarely longer than four or five links?
questions.model: Only about 10% of energy passes to the next level because most is lost as heat from respiration and in waste, so by the fourth or fifth level there is too little energy left to support another level.
questions.why: Energy loss limits food chain length.

panel.q: A predator's numbers rise after its prey increases. What happens next in a typical cycle?
o: Prey then fall as predators eat more
Prey then rise forever without any limit
Predators vanish at once from the area
Nothing changes in either population
panel.why: Predator–prey cycles are linked and lagged.

panel.q: Why do invasive species often spread quickly in a new habitat?
o: They may lack natural predators and diseases
They have no DNA, so they cannot be controlled
They are always larger than local species
The new habitat is empty of everything else
panel.why: Release from natural enemies lets numbers grow.

panel.q: Where does most of the biomass of an ecosystem lie?
o: In producers
In top predators
In decomposers only
In the air
panel.why: A pyramid of biomass narrows toward higher levels.

teach.topic: Why populations level off at a carrying capacity
teach.model: A population grows fast at first because resources are plentiful. As it grows, food, space and other resources become limited, and disease and competition increase. Births fall and deaths rise until the population levels off at the carrying capacity.

points.ask: How does it start?
What slows it down?
Where does it end up?

stages.title: Evolutionary biology
stages.hook: Finches on separate Galápagos islands have beaks of different shapes, yet are closely related. What can separate one species into two?
explain: Evolution by natural selection requires heritable variation, differences in survival or reproduction, and time. Other mechanisms change allele frequencies too: genetic drift (random change, strongest in small populations), gene flow (migration between populations) and mutation (the source of new alleles). The founder effect and bottlenecks are cases of drift.

A species is often defined as a group whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring. Speciation happens when populations become reproductively isolated. In allopatric speciation a geographic barrier separates populations, which then diverge by selection and drift. Reproductive barriers include different breeding times, courtship signals and hybrid sterility.

Evidence for evolution includes the fossil record, homologous structures (similar structure from common ancestry, like the limb bones of bats and whales), molecular similarity (DNA and proteins), biogeography, and observed evolution such as antibiotic resistance. Phylogenetic trees show inferred relationships: closely related species share a recent common ancestor.

example.q: In a population, 4% of individuals show a recessive trait (q² = 0.04). Using Hardy–Weinberg (p + q = 1), what is the frequency of heterozygotes (2pq)?

analogies.nature: Islands are like separate laboratories where populations evolve apart.
analogies.sport: Two teams that never play each other develop different tactics over the years.
analogies.tech: Software forks start from the same code and diverge as separate teams modify them.

stages.mnemonic: Mutation makes it, selection sorts it, drift shuffles it, isolation splits it.
terms: Random change in allele frequencies, strongest in small populations.
Formation of new species after geographic separation.
Similar structures from a common ancestor.
An organism's relative success at surviving and reproducing.

misc.wrong: Evolution is a ladder towards more advanced organisms.
misc.right: Evolution is a branching process with no goal. Organisms are adapted to their environment, not 'more advanced'.

stages.limits: Species definitions fail for asexual organisms and for groups that sometimes hybridise, so biologists use several concepts.

trip.prompt: Find an example of allopatric speciation and name the barrier that separated the populations.

questions.q: What is the original source of new alleles?
o: Mutation
Natural selection
Genetic drift
Migration
questions.why: Mutations create new alleles.

questions.q: Bat wings and whale flippers share a similar bone arrangement. This is evidence of:
o: Common ancestry (homologous structures)
Convergent evolution from identical genes
Chance alone producing similar bones
Direct inheritance of acquired traits
questions.why: Homology points to a common ancestor.

questions.q: In a population, 16% show a recessive trait (q² = 0.16). What is the frequency of the recessive allele q?
In a population of 100 individuals, 36 show a recessive trait (q² = 0.36). How many individuals are expected to be heterozygous?
The frequency of allele A is 0.7 in a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. What is the frequency of genotype AA?
Which process moves alleles between populations?
o: Gene flow
Mutation
Genetic drift
Speciation
questions.why: Migration of individuals carries alleles between populations.

questions.q: Order the steps in allopatric speciation.
items: A population is split by a barrier
Populations experience different selection and drift
questions.why: Isolation leads to divergence and eventual reproductive barriers.

questions.q: A storm leaves just ten birds of a species on a small island. Their allele frequencies differ from the original population by chance. This is:
o: The founder effect
Natural selection for fitness
Gene flow
Mutation
questions.why: A small founding group is not a representative sample.

questions.q: A student says 'the giraffe evolved a long neck because it needed to reach leaves'. Rewrite the explanation using natural selection.
questions.model: Giraffes varied in neck length. Those with longer necks reached more food, survived and reproduced more, passing on the alleles for longer necks, so over generations long necks became common. Need did not cause the change.
questions.why: Selection acts on heritable variation, not on need.

questions.q: Why is genetic drift more important in small populations than large ones?
o: Chance events have a larger relative effect on allele frequencies
Small populations do not mutate at all, so drift is stronger
Selection never acts in small populations
They have no alleles to change
questions.why: Sampling error is larger with few individuals.

panel.q: Why does hybrid sterility (like mules) help keep species distinct?
o: Hybrids cannot pass genes between the two species
Hybrids are bigger and so stronger than parents
Hybrids cannot walk or move around properly
It increases mutation in both species
panel.why: Blocking gene flow maintains species boundaries.

panel.q: A bacterium evolving antibiotic resistance during a patient's treatment is an example of:
o: Observed natural selection
Lamarckian inheritance of acquired traits
Speciation happening in a few minutes
Genetic drift acting alone
panel.why: Antibiotics select for resistant variants already present or arising by mutation.

panel.q: A phylogenetic tree shows A and B branching from a common point more recently than C. Which is true?
o: A and B are more closely related to each other than to C
C is the common ancestor of A and B
B evolved directly from A in the past
All three are equally closely related to each other
panel.why: Closeness is measured by the most recent common ancestor.

teach.topic: How a new species can form
teach.model: A population is split by a barrier such as a sea or mountain. The two groups no longer interbreed, so selection, drift and mutation make them different over time. Eventually they can no longer interbreed even if they meet again, so they are separate species.

points.ask: What starts the process?
What makes them change?
How do we know they are now different species?

stages.title: Experimental biology and biostatistics
stages.hook: A tablet group improved by 12% and a placebo group by 9%. Is the tablet working, or is it chance?
explain: A good experiment tests one independent variable, measures a dependent variable and controls other variables. A control group gives a baseline and random allocation reduces bias. Repeating measurements and using larger samples reduces the effect of chance. Reliable results can be repeated; valid results actually measure what was intended.

Descriptive statistics summarise data: the mean (sum ÷ number), median (middle value) and range. Standard deviation measures spread. Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Correlation does not prove causation: two variables can change together because of a third factor.

Hypothesis testing asks whether a result could easily happen by chance. A chi-squared test compares observed with expected counts: χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E. With one degree of freedom, a value above 3.84 gives p < 0.05, so the difference is called statistically significant. A p-value is the probability of results at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability the hypothesis is true.

example.q: A cross is expected to give a 3:1 ratio. From 100 offspring you observe 78 dominant and 22 recessive. Calculate χ² and decide if it fits at p = 0.05 (critical value 3.84, df = 1).
steps: 0.48 < 3.84, so the difference is not significant.

analogies.sport: A coin that lands heads 6 out of 10 times is not necessarily unfair; chance alone can give it.
analogies.farm: Testing a new fertiliser on one plot proves little; testing several plots with random assignment is stronger.
analogies.tech: A/B tests compare two versions of a website with random visitors.

stages.mnemonic: Change one, measure one, keep the rest the same.
terms: The claim that there is no effect or difference.
A result unlikely to be explained by chance alone.

misc.wrong: A small p-value proves the hypothesis is true.
misc.right: It shows the data would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true; it does not give the probability that the hypothesis is true or show the size of an effect.

stages.limits: Statistical significance depends on sample size, so a tiny effect can be significant in a huge sample, and a real effect can be missed in a tiny one.

trip.prompt: Find the example of a chi-squared test and check how the expected values were calculated.

questions.q: In an experiment on how light intensity affects plant growth, what is the dependent variable?
o: Plant growth
Light intensity
Temperature
Pot size
questions.why: Growth is what is measured.

questions.q: Plant heights (cm): 12, 15, 11, 14, 13. Which is the median?
questions.why: Sorted: 11, 12, 13, 14, 15; the middle value is 13.

questions.q: A yield rises from 40 to 50 kg per plot. What is the percentage increase?
A genetic cross is expected to give 3:1. From 200 offspring, 160 are dominant and 40 recessive. Calculate χ² (expected 150 and 50).
With χ² = 2.67, df = 1 and critical value 3.84 at p = 0.05, the conclusion is:
o: The difference is not significant
The difference is significant at p = 0.05
The cross is impossible to carry out
The sample is invalid and should be thrown away
questions.why: 2.67 is below 3.84, so chance could explain the difference.

questions.q: Why is a control group needed in a drug trial?
o: It gives a baseline to compare with
It receives the best new treatment on offer
It makes the trial shorter and cheaper
It removes the need for any statistics
questions.why: Without a baseline, change cannot be attributed to the drug.

questions.q: Order the stages of a scientific investigation.
items: Collect data in a controlled experiment
questions.why: Investigations move from question to conclusion.

questions.q: A result that can be repeated by others under the same conditions is:
o: Reliable
Valid
Biased
Random
questions.why: Reliability is repeatability.

questions.q: Ice cream sales and sunburn cases rise together. What is the best interpretation?
o: A third factor, hot sunny weather, may drive both
Ice cream causes sunburn directly
Sunburn causes more ice cream to be sold
They are completely unrelated and it is chance only
questions.why: Correlation does not prove causation; a confounding variable explains it.

questions.q: A student tests a fertiliser on one plant treated and one untreated. Explain two flaws and how to fix them.
questions.model: One plant per group is too small, so chance could explain the difference; use many plants and compare means. Other variables like light and water must be kept the same, and plants should be allocated to groups at random.
questions.why: Replication and control improve reliability and validity.

panel.q: A study of 20 000 people finds p = 0.03 for a tiny 0.1% difference. How should this be read?
o: Statistically significant but possibly not important in practice
Proof of a very large effect in people
Evidence of no effect whatever in the population
Invalid, because p is too small to count
panel.why: Large samples can detect very small differences, so effect size matters.

panel.q: Why is a double-blind design used in drug trials?
o: Neither participants nor researchers know who gets the treatment, which reduces bias
To save money by using fewer patients overall
To remove the control group from the trial
To make the results look bigger than they are
panel.why: Blinding reduces expectation effects.

panel.q: Results from three trials are 10, 11 and 30. Which is a better measure of the typical value?
o: Median, since the 30 is an outlier
Range, which shows how spread out the values are
Mean always, since it uses every value
Maximum, because it is the largest value
panel.why: The median is less affected by an outlier, though the outlier should be investigated.

teach.topic: How to design a fair test
teach.model: Change only one factor, the independent variable, and measure the result, the dependent variable. Keep everything else the same. Use a control group for comparison, repeat the measurements and use enough samples, then use a statistical test to see if the difference could be chance.

points.ask: What do you change?
What do you keep the same?
How do you know it isn't chance?
